topics.title: Emissions by source and net
topics.summary: Gross emissions are three things added together: what firms release directly in production, what households release directly (a fixed footprint per person), and what the power plants release when they burn fuel. The forest then absorbs some, and what is left is net emissions. Electricity use is not counted a second time at the firm or household: it is counted once, at the plant.
topics.formula: gross = firms (output x intensity x (1 - green tech)) + households (people x footprint) + plants (fossil energy delivered x emission factor); net = gross - forest sink

params.label: Direct footprint per person
params.unit: t CO2 per person per month

params.label: Emission factor of a fossil plant
Forest sink per unit of standing forest
params.unit: t CO2 per month per unit

examples.label: A Factory making 1,000 units a month with no green technology
The same Factory after 20% green technology
A fossil plant delivering 5 units of electricity in a month
A forest of 1,500 units
examples.note: The sink shrinks as the forest burns or is cleared.

topics.statusNote: Tuned for gameplay. A coal-like emission factor (about 1 t CO2 per MWh) is a rough real-world order of magnitude; the other figures are not calibrated to data.
leavesOut: Only CO2 is counted; no methane, no imports or exports of embodied carbon.
The whole town's footprint is one number; no transport, heating or diet detail.

topics.title: Power: demand, supply and rationing
topics.summary: Firms and households need electricity each month. Each plant has a fixed capacity. If the town wants more than the plants can supply, everyone is served in the same proportion and firms make less. Only fossil plants emit, so the cleaner the plant mix, the lower the emissions per unit of electricity.
topics.formula: demand = firms (output x energy per unit x (1 - green tech) x heat) + households; served = min(1, supply / demand); plant output = delivered x plant capacity / total capacity

params.label: Emission factor of a fossil plant
Extra demand per unit of drought severity

examples.label: Two fossil plants and one renewable plant
A Factory making 1,000 units with 20% green technology

topics.statusNote: The unit is called MWh but the capacities are game numbers chosen so that the starting town is near balance; they are not calibrated to real plants.
leavesOut: No grid: no transmission, storage, imports, prices or blackouts by area.
Plants do not wear out and never run at part load by choice.

topics.title: Grid and energy units
topics.summary: Electricity in the game is counted in MWh per month (the label comes from content). Capacity, demand, deliveries and household use are all in this one unit. Grid intensity is the tonnes of CO2 emitted per unit delivered: the fossil share of capacity times the fossil emission factor.
topics.formula: grid intensity = fossil capacity / total capacity x fossil factor (t CO2 per MWh); renewable share = renewable capacity / total capacity

params.label: Emission factor of a fossil plant

examples.label: One fossil plant of three
An all-renewable grid

topics.statusNote: Unit label only; magnitudes are game numbers.
leavesOut: No distinction between peak and average power, or between electricity and other energy.

topics.title: Household electricity needs
topics.summary: Each household wants a base amount of electricity per person plus an amount that grows with how much it spends. The need is based on last month's consumption. A drought raises it (cooling, pumping). If the grid cannot meet total demand, households are served in the same proportion as firms.
topics.formula: use = heat x people x (base per person + k x spending per person / reference spending)

params.label: Extra need at the reference spending
Extra demand per unit of drought severity

examples.label: A household of 3 spending $6,000 a month in total ($2,000 each)
The same household in a drought of severity 0.5 (heat = 1 + a_e x 0.5)
A household of 2 spending $1,000 a month in total

topics.statusNote: Invented to make households matter for emissions; not from household survey data.
leavesOut: No appliances, heating fuel or cars; one electricity number per household.

topics.title: Accumulated emissions and the carbon budget
topics.summary: Every month's net emissions are added to a running total. The game gives the town a fixed carbon budget for the whole run. The budget left is the budget minus the total so far. Warming is shown as a straight line from the starting temperature to the 1.5 C limit, reaching it exactly when the budget is gone. If cumulative emissions were ever negative they are held at zero.
topics.formula: cumulative = max(0, previous + net emissions); remaining = budget - cumulative; temperature = t0 + (limit - t0) x cumulative / budget

examples.label: After 450 t of cumulative emissions
After 450 t of cumulative emissions
After 450 t of cumulative emissions

topics.statusNote: The budget is scaled down so that a 40-turn game of a 20-person town can use it up. It is not a real-world carbon budget, and the temperature line is a game device, not a climate model.
leavesOut: No carbon cycle, no lag between emissions and warming, no other countries.

topics.title: Household spending and housing
topics.summary: A household spends part of its income and, slowly, some of its wealth. Spending is split between food, goods and services. Households pay rent for their home; when rent is too large a share of income for several months they can be evicted and look for somewhere cheaper. Rents drift up when homes are nearly full and down when they are empty.
topics.formula: spending = propensity (by class) x disposable income + wealth consumption; rent adjusts by a small step when occupancy passes a trigger

params.label: Share of non-food spending going to services
Share of wealth spent each month
Rent share of income that triggers distress
Months of unaffordable rent before eviction

topics.statusNote: Tuned for plausible shares; not calibrated to household budget data.
leavesOut: Eight households and seven homes: no housing market, mortgages, or moving between towns.

topics.title: Production and output
topics.summary: A firm makes output from its capital and from labour. Labour is the sum over its workers of skill times effective hours; effective hours fall with a long commute. The farm also depends on forest and commons health, climate damage and drought. Output is rationed if the grid falls short, and an emissions cap can limit it further.
topics.formula: output = productivity x capital^alpha x labour^beta, then x farm health, x climate factor, x drought factor (farm), x smoke factor, x electricity served

params.label: Farm output exponent on resource health
Farm output lost at the full carbon budget

examples.label: Productivity 1.0, capital 100 units, effective labour 50

topics.statusNote: Standard Cobb-Douglas shape with game-tuned exponents (alpha + beta = 1, constant returns); not estimated from data.
leavesOut: No intermediate goods, no technology choice beyond green investment, no imports.

topics.title: Wages, prices and profit
topics.summary: Firms pay wages first, then the carbon price and profit tax, then dividends to their owners. Wages drift with unemployment (a Phillips-curve style rule) and with skill. Prices move toward clearing the market: up when inventory runs low, down when it piles up. A firm that cannot cover wages pays what it can and falls behind.
topics.formula: wage moves by k x (reference unemployment - unemployment); price moves by an adjustment x inventory gap; profit = revenue - wages - interest - carbon cost - profit tax

params.label: Months of payroll kept as a cash reserve

topics.statusNote: Rules of thumb tuned until the town behaves plausibly; not estimated.
leavesOut: No bargaining, unions setting wages directly, or contracts; prices are not set by market power.

topics.title: GDP
topics.summary: GDP is what the town produces and sells in a month, put on a yearly footing. It adds firm sales, investment (capital that firms buy) and government services (public works, upkeep and the job guarantee). The headline figure is real GDP: nominal GDP divided by a price index, so price rises are not counted as growth.
topics.formula: GDP per year = 12 x (firm sales + investment + government services); real GDP = GDP / price index
topics.statusNote: The accounting definition is standard; the model's parts are simplified.
leavesOut: Unpaid work, housework and nature's services are not in GDP (GPI subtracts some of nature's costs).

topics.title: GPI (genuine progress indicator)
topics.summary: GPI starts from GDP and adjusts it for things GDP ignores. It is cut by inequality (a more unequal town counts for less), and by two costs: the social cost of the carbon emitted and the cost of natural capital used up (forest and commons lost). It can be much lower than GDP, or even negative.
topics.formula: GPI per year = GDP x (1 - Gini) - social cost of carbon x 12 x gross emissions - depletion cost x 12 x depletion

params.label: Cost of one unit of natural capital lost

examples.label: GDP of $600,000 a year, Gini 0.3, 12 t gross emissions and 2 units depleted in the month

topics.statusNote: The social cost of carbon is in the range of published estimates; the depletion price and the Gini weighting are game choices.
leavesOut: Leaves out unpaid work, leisure, health and many other items real GPIs include.

topics.title: Wage share and profit share
topics.summary: Wage share is the wages households receive divided by monthly GDP. Profit share is the profit of firms that made a profit divided by monthly GDP. They do not add to one: rent, interest, taxes and government services make up the rest. Both come with the dollar amounts they are made of.
topics.formula: wage share = wages paid to households / GDP; profit share = profits of profitable firms / GDP (both for the latest month)
topics.statusNote: Definitions are standard; the Finance tab also shows a labour-versus-profit split (wages / (wages + profit)), which is a different ratio.
leavesOut: Self-employment and owner income are folded into profit or dividends.

topics.title: Public debt over GDP
topics.summary: Public debt is what the government owes the bank. It is shown over a full year of GDP. When the ratio goes above one, legitimacy starts to drain. The government borrows when it spends more than it collects, within what the bank can lend, and repays part of any surplus.
topics.formula: debt / GDP = government debt / annual nominal GDP

params.label: Share of a surplus used to repay debt
Legitimacy lost per unit of debt/GDP above 1

examples.label: Debt of $300,000 with annual GDP of $600,000

topics.statusNote: Debt is only to the local bank; no bonds, no interest-rate risk beyond the bank's rate.
leavesOut: No foreign lenders, no central bank, no default by the government.

topics.title: Inequality (Gini)
topics.summary: The Gini coefficient measures how unequal wealth is: 0 means everyone has the same, 1 means one person has everything. In the game each person is given an equal share of their household's net worth, then the Gini is taken across all 20 people. The Lorenz curve shows the same thing as a picture. Net worth is savings plus homes and firm shares owned, minus debt.
topics.formula: Gini = sum over all pairs of people of |wealth_i - wealth_j| / (2 x people x total wealth), kept within 0..1

examples.label: Four people holding $10, $20, $30 and $40

topics.statusNote: The formula is the standard one; the wealth sharing inside a household is a simplification.
leavesOut: No income Gini; no distinction between wealth earned and inherited.

topics.title: Legitimacy
topics.summary: Legitimacy is the public's trust in the government, from 0 to 1. At zero the town collapses. Each month it goes up when people are doing well and goes down for high unemployment, high inequality, high public debt, a bank bailout, or switching economic system. Political capital to spend regenerates in proportion to it.
topics.formula: legitimacy = previous + w x (wellbeing - 0.5) - w x max(0, unemployment - threshold) - w x max(0, Gini - threshold) - w x max(0, debt/GDP - 1) - bailout penalty - switching resistance, kept within 0..1

params.label: Political capital regenerated per turn at full legitimacy

examples.label: Wellbeing 0.6, unemployment 15%, Gini 0.5, debt/GDP 1.2

topics.statusNote: Weights are game balance numbers; real legitimacy is not a single number.
leavesOut: No elections, parties or protests; the player simply governs until trust runs out.

topics.title: Bank capital ratio
topics.summary: The bank's capital ratio is its equity divided by its loans. The policy sets a minimum ratio; the bank cannot lend more than its equity divided by that ratio. Headroom is how many dollars it can still lend. A higher required ratio makes lending safer but limits credit and growth.
topics.formula: capital ratio = equity / loans; lending limit = equity / required ratio; headroom = limit - loans

examples.label: Equity of $50,000 with a 10% requirement

topics.statusNote: The idea follows capital rules for real banks; the numbers are game values.
leavesOut: One bank, no depositors who run, no interbank market.

topics.title: Money and credit
topics.summary: Money is bank deposits. When the bank lends, it creates a deposit; when a loan is repaid the deposit disappears. So lending creates money and repayment destroys it. Firms and the government borrow, with interest set by the base rate plus a spread that rises with leverage. Loans that are not repaid for several months are written off and cost the bank equity.
topics.formula: loan rate = base rate + spread (rises with leverage); deposits = money supply; write-off after N months without payment

params.label: Base spread over the policy rate
Extra spread per unit of leverage
Months before a loan is written off
Gap between loan and deposit rates
Share of bank profit paid to its owner

topics.statusNote: The money-creation mechanism follows how banks really work; the rates and terms are game values.
leavesOut: No central bank, no cash, no foreign money, no household credit (switched off).

topics.title: Income tax
topics.summary: Income tax (the lever key is tax_wage) is a flat rate on the wages households earn, including job-guarantee pay and public-works pay. It is collected monthly from savings; a household that cannot pay in full pays what it has.
topics.formula: income tax = rate x wages earned (paid only up to the household's savings)

examples.label: A rate of 15% on $8,000 of wages in a month

topics.statusNote: A flat rate; real income taxes are progressive and have allowances.
leavesOut: No tax-free allowance, no brackets, no tax on pensions separately.

topics.title: Profit tax
topics.summary: Profit tax is charged on a firm's profit before dividends (revenue minus wages, interest and carbon cost). Nothing is charged on a loss. Lobbying by owners can lower the rate in force below the rate you set.
topics.formula: profit tax = effective rate x max(0, revenue - wages - interest - carbon cost)

params.label: Largest share of a policy lobbying can remove

examples.label: A rate of 25% on $4,000 of pre-tax profit

topics.statusNote: A flat corporate tax; no loss carry-forward, depreciation allowances or avoidance.
leavesOut: No loss carry-forward, no tax havens.

topics.title: Capital tax
topics.summary: Capital tax is charged on what households receive from owning things: dividends from firms, rent from homes and interest. It is a flat rate on that income, collected monthly.
topics.formula: capital tax = rate x (dividends + rent received + interest received)
topics.statusNote: A flat rate on capital income; no distinction between kinds of capital income or capital gains.
leavesOut: No capital gains tax, no inheritance tax.

topics.title: Wealth tax
topics.summary: The wealth tax is an annual rate on a household's net worth above a threshold, collected in twelfths each month. Net worth is savings plus homes and firm shares, minus debt. Lobbying can weaken the rate in force.
topics.formula: monthly wealth tax = effective annual rate x max(0, net worth - threshold) / 12

examples.label: A household worth $200,000 with a $100,000 threshold and a 2% annual rate

topics.statusNote: The mechanism is standard; the threshold and rate ranges are game values.
leavesOut: No valuation problems or capital flight: wealth is measured exactly and cannot leave.

topics.title: Carbon price
topics.summary: The carbon price is dollars per tonne of CO2, charged to each firm on its footprint: its direct emissions plus the emissions of the electricity it uses. It reduces profit, so firms invest in green technology and cut output. The price in force can be lowered by lobbying. An emissions cap is a separate limit on a firm's footprint.
topics.formula: carbon payment = effective price x (direct emissions + energy use x grid intensity)

params.label: Green technology gained per investment step

examples.label: A price of $50 per tonne on a footprint of 10 t

topics.statusNote: The mechanism follows a carbon price; the response of firms is a simple rule.
leavesOut: Households do not pay a carbon price on their own footprint.

topics.title: GST / VAT: not modelled
topics.summary: The town has no sales tax. Adding one would change prices, demand and the ledger, so it is a possible future change rather than a setting. The government's tax money comes from income, profit, capital, wealth and carbon taxes.
topics.formula: There is no GST or VAT in the model.
topics.statusNote: Not modelled.
leavesOut: No sales tax, no tariffs, no excise duties.

topics.title: Policy, political capital and lobbying
topics.summary: Each change you make costs political capital and takes a few turns to start. Wealthy owners lobby against some policies: carbon price, profit tax, wealth tax and the emissions cap. The gap between the rate you set and the rate in force is the lobbying effect. Unions push back, and a campaign finance cap limits how much owners can spend. Cancelling a queued change refunds part of its cost.
topics.formula: effective policy = nominal x (1 - net lobbying pressure); cost = base x size of change x (1 + opposition)

params.label: Political capital regenerated per turn at full legitimacy
Share refunded when a queued change is cancelled
Share of income owners spend on lobbying

topics.statusNote: Lobbying strength and costs are game balance, not measured.
leavesOut: No parties, voters or legislature; lobbying is one number.

topics.title: Wages floor, benefits, basic income and job guarantee
topics.summary: The minimum wage sets a floor under what firms pay. Benefits go to unemployed adults and retired people. Basic income goes to every person. The job guarantee employs a share of the unemployed at the minimum wage in government jobs. All are paid monthly from taxes and borrowing; if the treasury cannot pay, payments are cut pro rata.
topics.formula: benefits = amount x eligible people; basic income = amount x people; job guarantee = minimum wage x people in the scheme

params.label: Months of public spending kept in cash

topics.statusNote: Amounts are game values; the schemes follow common designs.
leavesOut: No pensions system, no means testing or administration costs.

topics.title: Public spending, infrastructure and subsidies
topics.summary: The government buys goods and services from firms with the public spending lever (part to the Factory, part to the Shop). It pays upkeep on roads, public housing, power plants and fire stations and pays to build new ones, as wages to households. A green subsidy covers part of firms' green investment. Resilience spending lowers fire and drought risk.
topics.formula: goods bought = spending x (1 - services share); services bought = spending x services share; upkeep = count x upkeep per item

params.label: Share of public spending buying services

topics.statusNote: Costs and upkeep are round game numbers.
leavesOut: No procurement process, no waste, no cost overruns.

topics.title: Economic systems
topics.summary: The town runs under one of three systems: Market, Regulated or Co-op. Each changes which policies are available and how firms are owned and run (for example, worker co-ops share dividends among employees). Switching takes several months, costs political capital and drains legitimacy while it happens. No system gives the state a share of firms.
topics.formula: each system is a set of rules in content/systems/*.json; switching costs political capital and resistance
topics.statusNote: Systems are stylised ideal types, not descriptions of real countries.
leavesOut: No mixed economies in between and no state-owned firms in any system.

topics.title: Class and mobility
topics.summary: A household's class is worked out from where its income comes from and its skills: capitalists and rentiers live mainly on capital income, workers on wages, managers are skilled. Class sets how much of income is spent and how much political power a household has. A skilled household with savings may start a new firm when demand is strong.
topics.formula: class from the share of income that is capital income and skill; political power grows with wealth

params.label: Capital income share that makes a capitalist
Chance of changing class each month

topics.statusNote: Thresholds are game values; class is a label the model derives, not a measured category.
leavesOut: No inheritance, education or social networks.

topics.title: Forest and commons
topics.summary: The forest and the commons are stocks that regrow. The forest also absorbs carbon. The farm harvests both. A commons can be open, managed by the community with a cap, or enclosed by a wealthy owner who charges a fee. Building clears some forest. Health is the stock as a share of its maximum; the farm's output follows the average of the two.
topics.formula: growth = r x stock x (1 - stock / max) - harvest; forest sink = sigma x forest

params.label: Commons harvested per unit of farm output
Forest harvested per unit of farm output
Forest cleared per dollar of building

examples.label: A forest of 1,000 units

topics.statusNote: Logistic growth is the textbook shape; rates are game values.
leavesOut: No species, soils or water; two stocks stand for all of nature.

topics.title: Weather: climate stress, drought and fire
topics.summary: Climate stress is zero until the carbon budget remaining falls to an onset level and then rises to one as the budget runs out. Higher stress makes droughts and forest fires likelier and fiercer. A drought slows the commons, hurts the farm and raises electricity demand. A fire burns forest tiles, spreads to neighbours and costs output and wellbeing nearby. Fire stations and resilience spending cut the risk and the damage. A forecast shows the risk level.
topics.formula: stress = ((onset - remaining share) / (onset - full)) clamped to 0..1, raised to a curve exponent

params.label: Budget share left at which stress begins
Budget share left at which stress is full
Fire spread cut near a station

examples.label: After 450 t of cumulative emissions
After 800 t of cumulative emissions

topics.statusNote: The shape (more extreme weather as the budget runs out) is realistic; the numbers are game values.
leavesOut: No floods, storms or heat deaths; weather is only fire and drought.

topics.title: Wellbeing and unemployment
topics.summary: Wellbeing is a weighted mix of how well a person's consumption meets their needs, whether they have work, whether they are housed, the state of the environment and local smoke, and how secure their finances are. It moves slowly toward its target. Unemployment is the share of people in the labour force without a job; legitimacy uses a smoothed version.
topics.formula: wellbeing target = weighted sum of consumption, employment, housing, environment, security (less commute and smoke); unemployment = (labour force - employed) / labour force

params.label: Spending that meets a person's needs
Weight of the newest month in smoothed unemployment

topics.statusNote: Weights are a design choice; wellbeing is not measured against survey data.
leavesOut: No health, education, community or leisure.

topics.title: Winning and losing
topics.summary: The game lasts a fixed number of turns (each turn is a quarter, so 40 turns is ten years). You lose if the carbon budget runs out, if legitimacy falls to zero, if unemployment rises past the collapse level, or if a bank failure cascades. The first loss ends the game; surviving the last turn is a win, and the results screen scores the run.
topics.formula: outcome = the first of: budget exhausted, legitimacy 0, unemployment above the collapse level, bank cascade; otherwise survived
topics.statusNote: Thresholds are game design.
leavesOut: No partial credit for recovering after a crisis.

topics.title: What this model leaves out
topics.summary: This is a game about trade-offs in a small closed town, not a forecast. It has 20 people in 8 households, three firms, one bank and a government. It leaves out most of what makes a real economy and a real climate complicated, so use it to see how mechanisms interact, not to predict numbers.
topics.formula: (no formula)
topics.statusNote: All values in the game are tuned for play; see each topic for its status.
leavesOut: Trade and other towns: the economy is closed.
Births, deaths, ageing and migration: the population is fixed.
Other greenhouse gases and the global climate system.
Real-world data: nothing is calibrated.
Households' borrowing, housing markets, stock markets and a central bank.
Politics beyond one lever for lobbying and one number for legitimacy.

kinds.title: Households and people
kinds.summary: Eight households of people. A household decides how much of its money to spend each month and which shop gets it. People do not choose jobs one by one: firms hire from the unemployed (cheapest reservation wage first, ties to higher skill). A household's class is a label worked out from what it owns and earns; it is never chosen.
decides: How much to spend on food, goods and services this month
Which firm in each sector gets that spending
Whether to found a firm in the dormant slot (a Worker or Manager household with enough savings)
Capital-owning households: how much to give lobbying
observes: Its savings and last disposable income
The interest rate, firms' profit and unmet demand (for founding a firm)
kinds.rule: food = min(need x food price, savings); discretionary = min(propensity x max(0, disposable - food need) + wealth spending, savings - food); services = services share x discretionary; goods = the rest. Shop weight = stock x (average price / price) ^ elasticity, where the average price is weighted by stock

params.label: Share of discretionary spending on services
Capitalists and Rentiers: spending out of wealth
params.unit: share of net wealth per month

variants.label: Capitalist
variants.decision: Owns firms or the bank and lives mostly on profit; spends only part of income and funds lobbying.
variants.rule: owns assets and capital share of recent income above the threshold, rent not the main part

variants.label: Rentier
variants.decision: Lives mostly on rent from homes it lets; spends part of income and funds lobbying.
variants.rule: as Capitalist, but rent received is above the rentier share of capital income

variants.label: Manager
variants.decision: Skilled and well paid; spends most of income and is the person who receives lobbying money.
variants.rule: employed, top skill above the skill threshold and pay above the skilled wage ratio times the base wage

variants.label: Worker
variants.decision: Lives on wages; spends nearly all income, buying food first.

variants.label: Dependent
variants.decision: No one in the household has a job; lives on benefits and savings, food first.
variants.rule: no employed member, and not a Capitalist or Rentier

classParams.label: Capital share of income that makes a Capitalist or Rentier
Rent share of capital income that makes a Rentier
Pay needed for a Manager, against the base wage

kinds.title: Firms
kinds.summary: Factory, Farm and Shop, plus one dormant slot a household can start. Each firm decides how many workers it wants, what to pay and what to charge. (Market, Regulated and Coop are not kinds of firm: they are the town-wide economic system the player picks, which changes ownership and payout rules.)
decides: How many workers to have: hire up to a monthly cap, fire after a sustained surplus
The base wage, adjusted each month
How much to invest and borrow
observes: Expected sales (a smoothed average of past demand)
Its inventory and how much cover it wants
Its unit cost (wages plus carbon cost per unit)
kinds.rule: target workers = ceil(labour needed - hire slack), where needed output = expected sales x (1 + growth aspiration) + inventory adjust x (cover x expected sales - inventory); wage step = trend + wage_k x (u_ref - unemployment), capped; price moves a share of the way to (1 + markup) x unit cost; expected sales = smoothing x demand + (1 - smoothing) x previous

params.label: Share of the inventory gap closed per month
Largest wage change in a month
Share of the price gap closed per month
Weight of this month's demand in expected sales

kinds.title: Bank
kinds.summary: One bank that lends to firms against its equity, takes deposits and pays a dividend from excess capital. It follows a rule; it does not weigh individual borrowers.
decides: The interest rate each firm pays
How much a firm may borrow (a leverage cap and the bank's capital ratio)
How much of excess capital to pay out
observes: The base rate set by the player
Each firm's debt against its assets (leverage)
kinds.rule: firm loan rate = base rate + base spread + leverage spread x leverage + system spread; leverage = debt / (capital value + cash); borrowing limited to max leverage x assets

params.label: Base spread over the policy rate
Extra spread per unit of leverage
Share of excess capital paid out

kinds.title: Government
kinds.summary: The government collects taxes, pays benefits and spending and borrows for deficits, all at the levels the player sets. Its own rule is legitimacy: a score that drifts with wellbeing, unemployment, inequality and debt.
decides: Nothing on its own about policy: levers are the player's
How much to borrow or repay to keep a cash target
How much of its spending it can actually fund
observes: Wellbeing, smoothed unemployment, the Gini coefficient and debt against GDP
Whether the bank was bailed out this month
kinds.rule: legitimacy change = wellbeing weight x (wellbeing - 0.5) - unemployment weight x max(0, unemployment - threshold) - inequality weight x max(0, Gini - threshold) - debt weight x max(0, debt/GDP - 1) - bailout penalty

kinds.title: Lobbyists
kinds.summary: Not a separate body: Capitalist and Rentier households give a share of their capital income to the wealthiest Manager household, which acts as the lobbyist. Together with union density this erodes the policies the player sets. The player sees the nominal lever and the effective one.
decides: How much each capital-owning household gives (a share of capital income, up to its savings and the campaign cap)
observes: GDP, wage share and unemployment (for union strength)
kinds.rule: capital pull = lobby k x spend / monthly GDP, capped at the system's maximum; labour pull = union density x wage share x labour weight; net = clamp(capital - labour, 0, max); effective lever = nominal x (1 - net)

params.label: Influence per unit of spending against GDP
Largest net erosion of a lever

kinds.title: Nature
kinds.summary: Forest and commons are not agents: they follow fixed rules for growth, harvest and decay. The one chance event is an owner fencing off an open commons.
decides: Nothing: it responds to emissions, harvest and fire
observes: Cumulative emissions, forest stock, commons use and access rule
kinds.rule: see the Forest and commons topic for growth and the sink; enclosure is a monthly chance while the commons are open

params.label: Monthly chance of enclosure, Market system

kinds.title: Weather
kinds.summary: Droughts and fires are not decisions. Their odds rise with climate stress, which rises as the carbon budget runs down. They are the main place where the random seed matters.
decides: Nothing: odds follow climate stress, dryness and fire stations
observes: Climate stress, forest tiles, drought severity, fire station coverage
kinds.rule: drought chance = base x (1 + gain x stress); ignition chance = base x (1 + gain x stress) x dryness x standing share x (1 - resilience cut); spread chance = spread base x (1 + drought gain x severity) x (1 - station cut)

params.label: Base spread chance per neighbouring forest tile

randomness.probability: drought base x (1 + stress gain x climate stress), clamped to 0 to 1
randomness.when: each month with no drought running and climate stress above zero

randomness.event: How severe and how long a drought is
randomness.probability: two uniform draws on 0..1: severity = min(1, sev_min + u x (span base + span stress x stress)); months = dur_min + floor(u x (span base + span stress x stress))

randomness.event: A fire spreads to a neighbouring forest tile
randomness.probability: spread chance x (1 + drought gain x severity) x (1 - station cut if covered)
randomness.when: each month, once for each standing forest tile next to a burning tile

params.label: Cut inside a fire station's reach

randomness.probability: fire base x (1 + stress gain x stress) x dryness x standing forest share x (1 - resilience cut)
randomness.when: each month with climate stress above zero and some forest standing

randomness.probability: one uniform pick among the standing forest tiles
randomness.when: only when a new fire starts

randomness.event: A home next to a fire is damaged
randomness.probability: a fixed chance per home within one tile of a fire
randomness.when: each month for each such home; the draw happens only when the chance is above zero, and in the shipped content it is zero (off)

randomness.event: An owner fences off an open commons
randomness.probability: the economic system's enclosure chance; the richest Capitalist or Rentier household becomes the owner
randomness.when: each month while the commons are open and the chance is above zero (Market only in the shipped content)

randomness.event: A household founds a firm in the dormant slot
randomness.probability: mobility rate x max(0, sector return - base rate), clamped to 0..1
randomness.when: each month when a household has the savings and a dormant slot sits in a sector with enough unmet demand; one draw whatever the odds

params.label: Unmet demand needed in the sector

deterministic: Everything else is deterministic: spending, shop choice, hiring, wages, prices, credit, taxes, lobbying and legitimacy use no random draws.

The seed fixes one stream of random numbers. Changing it changes when droughts and fires happen and where, whether a commons is fenced off and whether a household founds a firm; it does not change the starting town.
The starting differences between households (income, savings, skill, who owns what) are written in content/initial_town.json, not drawn.
